Location Name: Basilica di San Marco (St. Mark's Basilica)
Description & Significance: Cathedral church of Venice and former Dogal chapel; world-renowned masterpiece of Italo-Byzantine and Gothic architecture with five gilded domes and over 8,000 square meters of gold ground mosaics.
Key Historical Context: Built to enshrine the relics of St. Mark the Evangelist translated from Alexandria in 828. Burned during the 976 anti-Candiano rebellion; rebuilt under Doge Domenico Selvo and consecrated in 1094. Houses the Pala d'Oro (1105/1345), the Quadriga bronze horses looted from Constantinople (1204), and the Nicopeia icon.

Specific Location / Address: Piazza San Marco (Western end, site of Ala Napoleonica)
Description & Significance: Historic Renaissance parish church that formerly closed the western side of Piazza San Marco facing the Basilica, designed by Jacopo Sansovino.
Key Historical Context: Legend attributed its foundation to Byzantine general Narses in 552. Rebuilt on the square's western edge by Cristoforo da Legname and Jacopo Sansovino. Demolished in 1807 by Napoleonic decree to build the Ala Napoleonica (ballroom and imperial palace wing); Sansovino was initially entombed here.

Description & Significance: Historic church flanking the northern side of St. Mark's Basilica in the Piazzetta dei Leoncini, now used as an auditorium and conference hall.
Key Historical Context: Founded by the Elia family in 1076. Severely damaged by urban fires in 1105 and 1661; rebuilt in classical baroque form in 1675 by architect Baldassarre Longhena. Suppressed under Napoleonic rule in 1806 and converted into an arms storehouse before restoration.

Description & Significance: Renaissance church renowned for its classical marble facade adorned with the bronze statue and scholarly inscriptions of patron Tommaso Rangone.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 9th century. Rebuilt in the High Renaissance by Jacopo Sansovino and Alessandro Vittoria, funded by physician-philologist Tommaso Rangone who placed his seated bronze monument above the portal. Houses works by Palma il Giovane and Veronese.

Description & Significance: Major Renaissance church of the Canons Regular of the Lateran, featuring a three-domed longitudinal Latin cross plan.
Key Historical Context: Legend holds it was founded following a vision seen by St. Magnus in the 7th century. Rebuilt by Giorgio Spavento and Tullio Lombardo, with Sansovino finishing the structural cloister and facade added by Giuseppe Sardi (1663). Houses Titian's celebrated 'Annunciation' and the monumental tomb of Queen Catherine Cornaro of Cyprus.

Description & Significance: Historic parish church near the Rialto Bridge that served as the parish for the neighboring German merchant community of the Fondaco dei Tedeschi.
Key Historical Context: Originally dedicated to San Demetrio in 840, rededicated in 1199. German merchants commissioned Albrecht Dürer in 1506 to paint the famous 'Feast of the Rosary' (*Festa del Rosario*) for its altar. Rebuilt in the 18th century by Giovanni Battista Scalfarotto; campanile built by Giovanni Scalfarotto in 1747–1754.

Description & Significance: Monumental Baroque church distinguished by an intensely sculpted, theatrical facade designed by Alessandro Tremignon and financed by patrician Vincenzo Fini.
Key Historical Context: Originally founded in the late 8th century; rededicated to Moses when patrician Moisè Venier rebuilt it in 960. Reconstructed in exuberant high baroque in 1682 featuring colossal bust portraits of the Fini family. Scottish financier John Law, founder of the Mississippi Company, was buried inside in 1729.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Zobenigo (Santa Maria del Giglio)
Specific Location / Address: Campo Santa Maria del Giglio, San Marco
Description & Significance: Baroque church famous for a lavish exterior marble facade completely devoid of Christian iconography, acting as a civic-military memorial for the Barbaro family.
Key Historical Context: Founded by the Jubbenico (Zobenigo) family in the 9th century. Rebuilt by Giuseppe Sardi between 1678 and 1681 at the expense of Admiral Antonio Barbaro; facade features carved relief maps of Zara, Candia, Padua, Rome, Corfu, and Spalato, and naval battle plans.

Specific Location / Address: Campo San Fantin (opposite Teatro La Fenice)
Description & Significance: Renaissance church standing directly opposite the Teatro La Fenice and adjacent to the Ateneo Veneto (Scuola di San Girolamo).
Key Historical Context: Founded in 996 by the Pisani, Barozzi, and Michiel families. Reconstructed in the 16th century by architects Antonio Abbondi (Scarpagnino) and Jacopo Sansovino, who completed the harmonious vaulted choir. Connected historically to the Scuola di San Fantin who comforted condemned criminals.

Description & Significance: Neoclassical Greek-cross church on Campo San Maurizio, now housing the Museo della Musica with historical instrument exhibitions.
Key Historical Context: Ancient foundation associated with the Candiano and Dandolo families. Rebuilt completely in 1806 by Giannantonio Selva and Antonio Diedo following the demolition of the decayed medieval and Sansovinesque church. Renowned for its connection to Venetian lutherie and Vivaldi.

Description & Significance: Historic church positioned at the northern approach of the Accademia Bridge, now a premier classical concert venue for Venetian chamber music.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1084 by Doge Vitale Falier. Rebuilt at the end of the 17th century by Andrea Tirali as a monument commemorating Doge Carlo Contarini. Houses Vittore Carpaccio's magnificent high altarpiece 'St. Vitalis on Horseback' (1514).

Description & Significance: Major Gothic monastic church of the Augustinians with a remarkable wooden ship's keel roof (*soffitto a carena di nave*) and an imposing leaning bell tower.
Key Historical Context: Erected by the Augustinian hermits on land purchased in 1294. Expanded in 1442 with an ornate flamboyant Gothic portal carved by Bartolomeo Bon. Doge Francesco Morosini (the 'Peloponnesiaco') is buried beneath a large bronze tomb slab in the central nave floor (1694). Canals flow directly underneath its presbytery.

Description & Significance: Parish church bordering the Grand Canal facing Palazzo Grassi, retaining its original 12th-century Romanesque-Veneto campanile.
Key Historical Context: Founded around the year 1000. Giacomo Casanova was baptized here in April 1725, as his parents were actors living in the parish; he later delivered his first sermons as an ecclesiastic here in 1740. Houses a 14th-century Gothic crucifix by Paolo Veneziano.

Description & Significance: Historic central parish church that occupied the center of Campo Sant'Angelo until its structural decay and demolition in the 19th century.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 920. In 1455, celebrated Bolognese architect Aristotele Fioravanti straightened its dangerously leaning bell tower using rollers, but the tower collapsed the next day due to foundation subsidence. Suppressed in 1810 and demolished in 1837.

Description & Significance: Intimate Baroque parish church standing in the campo alongside the Gothic Palazzo Fortuny (Pesaro degli Orfei).
Key Historical Context: Given to the Benedictines of San Michele di Brondolo in 1032. Reconstructed in 1685 by architect Baldassarre Longhena's circle following a structural collapse. Houses paintings by Bernardo Strozzi ('St. Sebastian Healed by the Holy Women') and Sebastiano Mazzoni.

Description & Significance: Parish church situated in the bustling commercial heart of Venice between Piazza San Marco and the Rialto, burial place of Pietro Aretino.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1072. Rebuilt at the end of the 16th century. Famed Renaissance writer, satirist, and playwright Pietro Aretino was buried here in 1556. Houses masterpieces by Paolo Veronese ('Virgin in Glory with St. Luke') and Palma il Giovane.

Description & Significance: Historic church and ancient five-sided Romanesque bell tower that formerly stood on the site of modern Campo Manin.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the late 9th century and dedicated to St. Paternian, Bishop of Bologna. Suppressed in 1810; demolished alongside its striking medieval pentagonal campanile in 1871 to erect the bronze monument to Venetian patriot Daniele Manin.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Croce degli Armeni
Description & Significance: National church and spiritual center of the historic Armenian merchant diaspora within the historic center of Venice.
Key Historical Context: Armenian merchants had established a commercial hostel and chapel in this alley off the Mercerie as early as the 13th century. Bequeathed by Armenian merchant Giorgio di Megerdich in the 17th century; remodeled in 1688 by Baldassarre Longhena. Still maintained by the Mechitarist Fathers.

Description & Significance: Small oratory and chapel located just north of the Procuratie Vecchie, originally built as an oratory for an adjacent hospice for poor pilgrims.
Key Historical Context: Erected in 1579 under Doge Nicolò da Ponte. Redesigned in 1703 by architect Matteo Lucchesi at the expense of the Gallo family. Houses paintings by Jacopo Tintoretto and his circle.

Location Name: Basilica dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo (San Zanipolo)
Description & Significance: Grand Dominican Gothic basilica known as the civic pantheon of the Venetian Republic; official burial site of 18 Doges and dozens of admirals and statesmen.
Key Historical Context: Granted to the Dominicans by Doge Jacopo Tiepolo in 1234 following a divine vision. Consecrated in 1430. Houses monumental tombs sculpted by Pietro, Tullio, and Antonio Lombardo, the preserved skin relic of Marcantonio Bragadin (1571), and the Cappella del Rosario.

Location Name: Cattedrale di San Pietro di Castello (Olivolo)
Specific Location / Address: Isola di San Pietro di Castello, Campo San Pietro
Description & Significance: Historic Cathedral of Venice and seat of the Bishop and Patriarch of Venice from 1451 until 1807, when St. Mark's became the official cathedral.
Key Historical Context: Founded on the ancient island of Olivolo in the 8th century. Rebuilt in Renaissance style with a facade designed by Andrea Palladio (1558) and executed by Francesco Smeraldi. Features the ancient marble Chair of St. Peter ('Cattedra di San Pietro') and Mauro Codussi's leaning Istrian stone bell tower (1482–1488).

Description & Significance: Prominent monastic church and convent of Benedictine noble nuns with a transitional Gothic-Renaissance facade by Antonio Gambello and Mauro Codussi.
Key Historical Context: Founded under Doge Angelo Partecipazio to house relics of St. Zechariah. The convent had immense wealth and doges made annual Easter processions here. Buried eight early doges. Features a submerged Romanesque crypt and Giovanni Bellini's famous San Zaccaria Altarpiece (1505).

Location Name: Chiesa di San Francesco della Vigna
Specific Location / Address: Campo San Francesco della Vigna, Castello
Description & Significance: Monumental Franciscan Renaissance church commissioned by Doge Andrea Gritti, featuring a harmonious harmonic-proportion interior by Jacopo Sansovino and a facade by Andrea Palladio.
Key Historical Context: Built on land donated by Marco Ziani containing a historic vineyard ('vigna'). Sansovino laid out the interior following Kabbalistic and neo-Platonic proportional theories formulated by Franciscan friar Francesco Zorzi. Palladio designed the triumphal facade in 1562. Houses works by Veronese and Giovanni Bellini.

Description & Significance: Renaissance church on a grand campo, designed by Mauro Codussi on the foundations of a 7th-century church, famous for its two external facades.
Key Historical Context: Legend says St. Magnus was guided by an apparition of the Virgin Mary appearing as a shapely woman ('formosa'). Reconstructed in 1492 by Mauro Codussi. Historically tied to the Festa delle Marie (abduction of the brides in 944) and the guild of the Casseleri (box-makers). Houses Palma il Vecchio's St. Barbara altarpiece.

Location Name: Chiesa della Pietà (Santa Maria della Visitazione)
Description & Significance: Celebrated 18th-century church renowned as the church and music academy of Antonio Vivaldi and the orphan girls' choir of the Ospedale della Pietà.
Key Historical Context: Founded adjacent to the historic foundling hospital. Designed by architect Giorgio Massari with exceptional acoustic engineering (oval chamber). Features ceiling frescoes by Giambattista Tiepolo ('Triumph of Faith'). Completed with a neoclassical facade in 1906.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giorgio dei Greci
Description & Significance: The cathedral church of the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Italy, featuring a prominent leaning campanile and rich Post-Byzantine Cretan icons.
Key Historical Context: Constructed with Senate permission by the affluent Greek expatriate and refugee community following the fall of Constantinople. Designed by Sante Lombardo and Giannantonio Chiona; consecrated in 1573. Decorated with icons by Michael Damaskinos.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giovanni in Bragora
Description & Significance: Charming late-Gothic parish church in Campo Bandiera e Moro where composer Antonio Vivaldi was baptized in 1678.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 9th century. Rebuilt in brick late Gothic style in the late 15th century by Sebastiano da Lugano. Preserves the baptismal font of Antonio Vivaldi (March 1678) and Pietro Bembo. Houses Cima da Conegliano's masterpiece 'Baptism of Christ' on the high altar.

Description & Significance: Parish church of the Venetian naval shipwrights (*Arsenalotti*), designed by Jacopo Sansovino with a square centralized plan.
Key Historical Context: Founded by refugees from Altinum. Reconstructed in the 16th century by Jacopo Sansovino. The church was intimately connected to the Arsenal workers, who maintained altars and guild funerary stones here. Contains the tomb of Doge Francesco Erizzo (1646).

Location Name: Chiesa di San Biagio Vescovo (ai Forni)
Description & Significance: Historic naval parish church and parish of the grain bakers (*ai Forni*), now serving as the official military chapel of the Italian Navy.
Key Historical Context: Originally served the Dalmatian and Greek sailors. Rebuilt in the mid-18th century by Filippo Rossi. Houses the funerary monument of Austrian Admiral Archduke Frederick Ferdinand of Habsburg (died 1847).

Description & Significance: Historic neighborhood church standing at a busy pedestrian junction between San Zaccaria and the Arsenale.
Key Historical Context: Founded by the patrician Badoer family in the 9th century. Reconstructed in 1680 by architect Baldassarre Longhena. Features the Cappella Savorgnan with paintings by Sebastiano Ricci and Palma il Giovane.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giovanni Nuovo (San Zaninovo)
Description & Significance: Neoclassical church tucked inside Campo San Giovanni Novo, designed by Matteo Lucchesi based on Palladian models.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 968. Completely rebuilt in 1762 by architect Matteo Lucchesi with a single rectangular hall inspired by Palladio's Redentore. Known as 'San Zaninovo' to distinguish it from the larger San Giovanni in Bragora and San Giovanni Crisostomo.

Description & Significance: Enormous monastic church and wealthy Benedictine convent where traveler Marco Polo was interred in 1324; now an ocean sound and art exhibition center (Ocean Space).
Key Historical Context: One of Venice's oldest monasteries, founded by the Partecipazio family. Rebuilt by Simone Sorella between 1592 and 1602 with a massive dual-room layout separated by iron grates for cloistered nuns. Marco Polo was buried in the convent church in 1324 (tomb lost during renovations).

Description & Significance: Former Augustinian convent church whose baroque facade was erected as a lavish monument to the Procurator Nicolò Soranzo.
Key Historical Context: The Venetian state honored St. Justina because the victory of Lepanto occurred on her feast day (October 7, 1571); doges visited the church annually on that date. Rebuilt by Baldassarre Longhena in 1640. Suppressed under Napoleon in 1810 and today houses the Liceo Scientifico G.B. Benedetti.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giuseppe di Castello (Sant'Isepo)
Description & Significance: Augustinian monastic church bordering the eastern end of Via Garibaldi, retaining a conventual raised wooden choir (*barco*) across its entrance.
Key Historical Context: Authorized by Senate decree in 1512 for Augustinian nuns. Houses the monumental tomb of Doge Marino Grimani and his wife Dogaressa Morosina Morosini, designed by Vincenzo Scamozzi with bronze reliefs by Girolamo Campagna.

Description & Significance: Gothic monastic church located on the eastern tip of Venice, dedicated to Empress St. Helena whose relics were brought here from the Levant in 1211.
Key Historical Context: Constructed by Olivetan monks. In 1476, Antonio Rizzo designed the splendid Renaissance portal surmounted by the monument to Captain Vittore Cappello. Suppressed under Napoleon in 1810; reconsecrated in 1928 under the Servite order.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Consolazione (della Fava)
Description & Significance: Baroque church of the Congregation of the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri, designed by Antonio Gaspari and Giorgio Massari.
Key Historical Context: Originally housed a miraculous image of the Madonna della Consolazione placed near a bridge where fava bean merchants operated. Rebuilt in the 18th century. Preserves Giovanni Battista Piazzetta's celebrated 'Virgin with St. Philip Neri' and young Giambattista Tiepolo's 'Education of the Virgin'.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Pianto
Specific Location / Address: Fondamente Nove / Rio di Santa Giustina
Description & Significance: Octagonal central-plan Baroque church designed by Baldassarre Longhena for the Servite nuns during the War of Candia.
Key Historical Context: Erected by decree of the Venetian Senate in 1649 as a votive sanctuary praying for divine protection during the grueling 25-year Ottoman siege of Candia (Crete). Suppressed under the French in 1810 and long incorporated into civil hospital wards.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria dei Derelitti (Ospedaletto)
Description & Significance: Church of one of the four great welfare hospitals of Venice, famous for its grotesque, muscular Baroque facade sculpted by Baldassarre Longhena and Giuseppe Sardi.
Key Historical Context: Founded during the 1528 famine to care for destitute orphans and derelicts. Features an exuberantly theatrical facade adorned with giant stone atlantes and weeping telamons funded by merchant Bartolomeo Cargnoni. Renowned for its elliptical music room designed by Jacopo Guarana.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Lazzaro dei Mendicanti
Description & Significance: Hospital church designed by Vincenzo Scamozzi, integrated into the grand complex of the Ospedale Civile adjacent to the Basilica di San Zanipolo.
Key Historical Context: Constructed to serve the hospital for beggars and lepers established by the Republic. Facade completed by Giuseppe Sardi in 1673 based on Scamozzi's designs, featuring the monument to naval captain Alvise Mocenigo. Houses paintings by Veronese and Tintoretto.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giovanni Battista del Tempio (dei Cavalieri di Malta)
Specific Location / Address: Corte San Giovanni di Malta, Castello
Description & Significance: Historic priory church of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta in Venice, originally founded by the Knights Templar.
Key Historical Context: Given to the Templars in 1187 by Doge Orio Mastropiero. Transferred to the Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem (Malta) in 1312 upon the papal dissolution of the Templar order. Contains tombs of Grand Priors and naval knights.

Description & Significance: Ancient monastic church and Benedictine convent destroyed during 19th-century urban redevelopments.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the early 9th century. Damaged in the 1105 fire; later rebuilt in the 16th century. Suppressed under the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy in 1806, converted into a military prison, and completely demolished in 1829.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Ternita (Santissima Trinità - demolished 1810)
Description & Significance: Historic parish church of the Knights of the Teutonic Order, demolished under French military rule.
Key Historical Context: Granted to the Teutonic Knights in the 13th century. Reconstructed in the early 16th century. Suppressed in 1806 and demolished in 1810; the site is today an open residential square (Campo Santa Ternita).

Description & Significance: Parish church famous as the civic celebration site for the recapture of Padua in 1509 during the War of the League of Cambrai.
Key Historical Context: Relics of St. Marina were stolen from Constantinople in 1206 and placed here. Because Padua was liberated on her feast day (July 17, 1509), the Doge visited in solemn annual procession. Buried Doges Nicolò Marcello and Michele Steno (whose tombs were moved to San Zanipolo when the church was razed in 1820).

Location Name: Chiesa di San Procolo (San Provolo - demolished 1814)
Description & Significance: Early medieval parish church near San Zaccaria demolished in the early 19th century.
Key Historical Context: Destroyed in the great fires of 1105; rebuilt in Renaissance style in the 16th century. Suppressed in 1808 and demolished in 1814.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria delle Vergini (demolished late 19th C.)
Specific Location / Address: Rio delle Vergini (Northern edge of Arsenale)
Description & Significance: Venerable aristocratic Augustinian convent church whose abbess was personally consecrated by the Doge.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1224 by Doge Pietro Ziani. The convent enjoyed the unique privilege of dogal patronage. Suppressed under Napoleon; demolished during Italian naval expansions to enlarge the docks and coal basins of the Arsenale.

Specific Location / Address: Near Rio delle Vergini / Lake San Daniele
Description & Significance: Ancient Augustinian monastic church located on the marshy lagoon lake that was excavated in 1303 to build the Arsenale Nuovo.
Key Historical Context: Given to the Cistercian order in the 13th century. Suppressed in 1806 and demolished in 1839 to make room for barracks and naval storehouses.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Domenico di Castello (demolished 1807)
Description & Significance: Monumental Dominican monastery and church that served as the primary seat of the Venetian Holy Office (Inquisition).
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1317. Rebuilt in the 16th century with paintings by Tintoretto and Palma. Razed to the ground by Napoleon Bonaparte in 1807 to lay out the public park of the Giardini di Castello.

Location Name: Chiesa di Sant'Antonio Abate di Castello (demolished 1807)
Specific Location / Address: Punta di Quintavalle / Giardini di Castello
Description & Significance: Large monastic church of the Canons Regular of St. Anthony, celebrated for its 12 private patrician chapels.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1346 by Fra Giotto degli Abbati. Remodeled in 1480 by Mauro Codussi. Held tombs of Doges Cristoforo Moro and Nicolò Tron. Demolished under Napoleon in 1807 along with San Domenico to clear the land for the Giardini di Castello.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Nicolò di Castello (demolished 1807)
Description & Significance: Parish church serving the mariners and salt-workers of eastern Castello until its demolition under the French.
Key Historical Context: Destroyed alongside San Domenico and Sant'Antonio in 1807 to create the public promenade of the Giardini Napoleonici.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giovanni Battista dei Furlani
Description & Significance: Small chapel and hospice church belonging to the Friulian national guild (*Scuola dei Furlani*).
Key Historical Context: Erected by immigrants from Friuli (*Furlani*) to care for needy workers and organize religious festivals honoring Saint John the Baptist.

Description & Significance: Exemplary Venetian Gothic church originally built by the Umiliati; parish church, museum, and burial place of Jacopo Tintoretto.
Key Historical Context: Originally dedicated to San Cristoforo. Rededicated after Giovanni De Santi's stone statue of Virgin & Child in a nearby garden (orto) emitted mysterious glows and was brought inside on June 18, 1377. Rebuilt after a 1399 collapse. Jacopo Tintoretto, Marietta, and Domenico are interred inside.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria dei Miracoli
Description & Significance: Early Renaissance architectural jewelbox designed by Pietro Lombardo, completely clad inside and outside in polychrome patterned marbles.
Key Historical Context: Erected to enshrine a miraculous image of the Virgin painted on a panel by Nicolò di Pietro in 1408 that had reputedly resurrected a drowned woman. Famous for its raised presbytery and barrel-vaulted coffered wooden ceiling.

Description & Significance: Monumental Baroque church of the Society of Jesus, famous for its interior marble inlay mimicking draped green and white damask curtains.
Key Historical Context: Originally occupied by the hospitaller order of the Crociferi. Purchased by the Jesuits in 1657 upon their return from exile; rebuilt by Domenico Rossi with funding from the Manin family. Houses Titian's dramatic 'Martyrdom of Saint Lawrence' and Tintoretto's 'Assumption'.

Location Name: Chiesa degli Scalzi (Santa Maria di Nazareth)
Description & Significance: Grand Venetian Baroque church of the Discalced Carmelite friars (*Carmelitani Scalzi*), designed by Baldassarre Longhena with a facade by Giuseppe Sardi.
Key Historical Context: Carmelites arrived from the Holy Land and established this convent in the 17th century. The magnificent vault fresco of the Transport of the Holy House of Loreto painted by Giambattista Tiepolo was destroyed by an Austrian aerial bomb on October 24, 1915. Lodovico Manin, last Doge of Venice, was buried here in 1802.

Description & Significance: Early Renaissance Franciscan church designed by Pietro Lombardo, renowned for the glazed Della Robbia terracotta roundels in its Martini Chapel.
Key Historical Context: Built adjacent to a plague hospital under Doge Cristoforo Moro (who is buried here). Pietro Lombardo carved the elegant Renaissance portal and interior relief sculpture. Giovanni Bellini and Vittore Carpaccio painted landmark altarpieces for this church (now in the Accademia).

Location Name: Chiesa di San Geremia e Santa Lucia
Description & Significance: Prominent church at the junction of the Grand Canal and Cannaregio Canal, housing the intact body and pilgrimage shrine of Saint Lucy of Syracuse.
Key Historical Context: Rebuilt in 1753 by Carlo Corbellini. When the nearby medieval church of Santa Lucia was demolished in 1861 to build the railway station, the incorrupt body of Saint Lucy was translated to San Geremia, where she remains enshrined in a dedicated chapel.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Marcuola (Santi Ermagora e Fortunato)
Description & Significance: Grand Canal parish church designed by Giorgio Massari with an unfinished brick facade, known locally by the Venetian contraction 'San Marcuola'.
Key Historical Context: Dedicated to the patriarchal martyrs of Aquileia, Hermagoras and Fortunatus. Reconstructed in the 18th century by Massari with a rich Rococo interior. Houses Jacopo Tintoretto's celebrated 'Last Supper' (1547).

Description & Significance: High Renaissance church standing on the Strada Nova, built on a centralized Greek-cross plan attributed to the workshop of Mauro Codussi.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 10th century. Rebuilt in 1531. Noted for its harmonious classical spatial balance and Jacopo Tintoretto's youthful masterpiece 'Saint Demetrius in Arms'.

Description & Significance: Ancient parish church tucked behind the Strada Nova near the Grand Canal traghetto, giving its name to Palazzo Santa Sofia (Ca' d'Oro).
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 9th century. Rebuilt in the late 17th century by architect Antonio Gaspari. Truncated in the 19th century when the Strada Nova pedestrian artery was cut across Cannaregio.

Description & Significance: One of the earliest Christian foundations in Venice, housing the Renaissance burial chapel of the Corner family (*Cappella Corner*).
Key Historical Context: Tradition names it as one of the eight churches founded by Saint Magnus. Rebuilt in 1575 by Alessandro Vittoria. The magnificent Cappella Corner, built by Mauro Codussi (1490), houses the tomb of Marco Corner (father of Queen Catherine Cornaro) and Giambattista Tiepolo's 'Communion of St. Lucy' (1748).

Description & Significance: Parish church dedicated to the 4th-century Aquileian martyr siblings Cantianus, Cantianilla, and Cantius.
Key Historical Context: Founded by refugees from the mainland in the 9th century. Rebuilt in the 14th century and given its present interior in the early 18th century, funded by patrician Michele Rachetti. Contains the Rachetti chapel with sculptures by Giuseppe Bernardo and paintings by Domenico Zanchi.

Description & Significance: Masterpiece of High Renaissance centralized architecture, the final work designed by Mauro Codussi.
Key Historical Context: Destroyed by a fire in 1475; rebuilt between 1497 and 1504 on a Greek-cross plan by Mauro Codussi and finished by his son Domenico. Houses Sebastiano del Piombo's magnificent high altarpiece (1510) and Giovanni Bellini's last signed altarpiece depicting Saints Jerome, Christopher, and Augustine (1513).

Location Name: Chiesa di Sant'Alvise (San Ludovico da Tolosa)
Description & Significance: Gothic monastic convent church standing on the quiet northern lagoon edge of Cannaregio, renowned for its dramatic paintings by Giambattista Tiepolo.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1388 by Antonia Venier following an apparition of St. Louis of Toulouse (*Alvise*). Preserves its original elevated nuns' hanging choir (*barco*) supported by Gothic columns and three monumental Passion canvases by Giambattista Tiepolo ('The Road to Calvary', 'The Flagellation', and 'The Crowning with Thorns').

Description & Significance: Baroque parish church celebrated for its gilded wood-carved ceiling frames and dynamic canvases by Tintoretto and Sebastiano Ricci.
Key Historical Context: Dedicated to Saint Martial, Bishop of Limoges. Rebuilt in the late 17th century by architect Andrea Cominelli. Ceiling is completely covered in carved gilded frames containing paintings by Sebastiano Ricci (1700); also houses Tintoretto's famous 'Saint Martial in Glory'.

Description & Significance: Parish church facing the Strada Nova with a towering neoclassical facade designed by Domenico Rossi.
Key Historical Context: Ancient foundation; rebuilt following a catastrophic fire in 1733 by Domenico Rossi. The church looks out onto the bronze monument of Servite friar, theologian, and scientist Paolo Sarpi (who was assassinated on the adjacent Ponte dei Servi in 1607).

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Misericordia (Abbazia)
Description & Significance: Former Augustinian abbey church terminating the picturesque canal and campo of the Scuola Vecchia della Misericordia.
Key Historical Context: Rebuilt in 1659 with an elaborate Baroque facade designed by Clemente Moli and financed by patrician Gaspare Moro. Secularized in the late 19th century and long used for art restoration studios before being restored for Biennale exhibitions.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria dei Servi (partially demolished)
Description & Significance: Formerly one of the largest and grandest Gothic churches in Venice, home convent of state theologian Fra Paolo Sarpi.
Key Historical Context: Begun in 1318 by the Servite order. Stretched over 100 meters in length and contained lavish chapels of the noble families. Razed to the ground following Napoleonic suppression in 1813, leaving only the Gothic entrance portal, the Cappella dei Lucchesi, and monastery perimeter walls.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Maddalena (La Maddalena)
Description & Significance: Remarkable Neoclassical circular temple church designed by architect Tommaso Temanza, inspired by the Pantheon in Rome.
Key Historical Context: Patronage belonged to the Baffo and Balbi families. Rebuilt by Temanza on an innovative circular plan with a dome, featuring Masonic and esoteric symbols carved into the triangular pediment above the entrance portal.

Description & Significance: Historic church positioned on the wide market square of Campo San Leonardo, now secularized and functioning as a civic hall.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 11th century. Rebuilt in neoclassical form in 1794 by architect Bernardo Maccaruzzi. Closed to worship under Napoleon in 1810 and stripped of furnishings; later served as a cinema and municipal auditorium.

Description & Significance: Monastic church and convent situated alongside the Rio di San Girolamo in northern Cannaregio.
Key Historical Context: Damaged by severe fires in 1434 and 1705; reconstructed in the 18th century by architect Domenico Rossi. Suppressed in 1806 under the French and used as a factory and warehouse before undergoing civic restoration.

Location Name: Chiesa delle Cappuccine (Santa Maria degli Angeli)
Description & Significance: Quiet monastic church and convent established by the Capuchin Poor Clare nuns in northern Cannaregio.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the early 17th century by Mother Maria Angela Suardi. Features a simple Franciscan single-nave structure dedicated to prayer and charity, retaining its cloister and vegetable gardens along the northern lagoon.

Specific Location / Address: Site of Venezia Santa Lucia Railway Station
Description & Significance: Historic conventual church that preserved the relics of Saint Lucy until its demolition to construct the central railway station.
Key Historical Context: Relics of Saint Lucy were brought here following the sack of Constantinople in 1204. Rebuilt in Renaissance style with a portal designed by Andrea Palladio. Suppressed in 1806 and demolished in 1861 under Austrian rule to lay tracks for the railway terminal, giving the station its name (Venezia Santa Lucia).

Specific Location / Address: Western edge of Santa Lucia Station
Description & Significance: Augustinian Dominican convent church famous for the religious reforms of Blessed Giovanni Dominici.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1394 by noblewoman Lucia Tiepolo. Fra Giovanni Dominici promoted a major reform movement of the Dominican order here in 1399. Razed to the ground in 1810 under the French occupation.

Description & Significance: Monastic church and convent founded by the Reformed Minorites (Franciscan Reformed friars).
Key Historical Context: Built on the secluded northern boundary of Venice. Houses works by Jacopo Tintoretto and Leonardo Corona, preserving an austere Franciscan conventual spirit.

Location Name: Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari
Description & Significance: Grand Franciscan Gothic basilica and one of Venice's greatest architectural monuments, measuring over 100 meters long, with the second-tallest campanile in the city.
Key Historical Context: Erected by the Franciscan Minor Friars (*Frati Minori*). Houses Titian's breathtaking masterpiece 'The Assumption of the Virgin' (*Assunta*, 1518) and 'Pesaro Madonna', alongside Donatello's wooden statue of St. John the Baptist, Bellini's Frari Triptych, and the monumental tombs of Titian, Antonio Canova, and Doge Francesco Foscari.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giacomo di Rialto (San Giacometo)
Specific Location / Address: Campo San Giacomo di Rialto (Foot of Rialto Bridge)
Description & Significance: Traditionally held as the oldest church in Venice, distinguished by its medieval portico and monumental 24-hour clock face over the Rialto market square.
Key Historical Context: Venetian myth dates its foundation to the legendary founding of Venice on March 25, 421. Stood at the commercial nerve center of the Rialto banking district, carrying an inscription urging merchants to be honest and deal fairly. Survived the catastrophic Rialto fire of 1514 untouched.

Description & Significance: High Renaissance church embedded into the market stalls of the Rialto, designed by Antonio Abbondi (Scarpagnino) following the 1514 Rialto fire.
Key Historical Context: Burned to ashes during the great Rialto commercial fire of January 1514. Scarpagnino designed a masterful Renaissance Greek-cross plan hidden behind market shops. Houses Titian's luminous altarpiece of 'Saint John the Almsgiver' (1545) and frescoes by Il Pordenone.

Specific Location / Address: Campo San Rocco (beside Scuola Grande di San Rocco)
Description & Significance: Confraternity church of the Scuola Grande di San Rocco, dedicated to the patron saint of plague victims whose relics rest in the high altar.
Key Historical Context: Designed by Bartolomeo Bon and consecrated in 1508. Acquired the holy relics of Saint Roch in 1485. Facade rebuilt in neoclassical style by Bernardino Maccaruzzi in 1771. Filled with magnificent narrative canvases by Jacopo Tintoretto depicting the miracles and passion of Saint Roch.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Polo (San Paolo Apostolo)
Description & Significance: Major parish church anchoring the expansive open square of Campo San Polo, with a Gothic ship's keel roof and a 14th-century Romanesque campanile.
Key Historical Context: Founded under Doge Pietro Tradonico in the 9th century. Given a lavish Gothic interior in the 15th century and a southern portal sculpted by Bartolomeo Bon. Contains Giambattista Tiepolo's 'The Virgin Appearing to Saint John Nepomuk' and Tintoretto's 'Last Supper'.

Description & Significance: Historic parish church near the Grand Canal, renowned as an art treasure-house containing three monumental paintings by Jacopo Tintoretto.
Key Historical Context: Originally dedicated to Saint Cecilia in the 8th century, rededicated to Saint Cassian in 926. Rebuilt in the 17th century. Preserves Jacopo Tintoretto's celebrated 'Crucifixion' (1568), 'Resurrection', and 'Descent into Limbo'.

Description & Significance: Late Gothic parish church featuring a tall pointed-arch facade decorated with 13th-century Byzantine marble roundels.
Key Historical Context: Founded by families from Ravenna in the 11th century. Reconstructed in Gothic style in the 15th century. Closed to worship in the 19th century and long served as a state archive storehouse.

Description & Significance: Parish church historically tied to the Patriarchate of Grado, standing near the Grand Canal between Rialto and San Polo.
Key Historical Context: Historic seat of the Patriarchs of Grado after they relocated to Venice in 1156. Rebuilt in neoclassical style by Lorenzo Santi in the 19th century. Preserves Tintoretto's luminous 'Baptism of Christ' (1580).

Description & Significance: Parish church bordering the Traghetto di San Tomà on the Grand Canal, directly facing the Scuola dei Calegheri (Shoemakers' Guild).
Key Historical Context: Reconstructed in the 18th century by architect Francesco Bognolo. The square was home to the shoemakers' confraternity, whose carved relief of Saint Mark healing the shoemaker Anianus adorns the opposite guildhall.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Boldo (San Ubaldo - demolished 1808)
Description & Significance: Parish church that stood in Campo San Boldo until its demolition under French rule; its 14th-century bell tower base survives incorporated into a palazzo.
Key Historical Context: Dedicated to Saint Ubaldus (corrupted into 'San Boldo'). Burned down in 1105 and rebuilt in the 14th century. Suppressed and demolished in 1808.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Stin (San Stefanino - demolished 1810)
Description & Significance: Historic parish church whose memory survives in the name of Campo San Stin near the Frari.
Key Historical Context: Dedicated to Saint Stephen Protomartyr (diminutive 'Stefanino' / 'Stin'). Suppressed in 1806 and demolished in 1810 to widen public pedestrian thoroughfares.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Matteo di Rialto (demolished 1807)
Description & Significance: Small parish church embedded in the vegetable and poultry markets of the Rialto.
Key Historical Context: Served the butcher and market trader guilds of Rialto. Suppressed in 1806 and razed to expand the market stalls.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Nicola da Tolentino (I Tolentini)
Description & Significance: Monumental church of the Theatine Order, designed by Vincenzo Scamozzi with a grand Roman Corinthian temple portico added by Andrea Tirali.
Key Historical Context: The Theatines settled here following the 1527 Sack of Rome. Scamozzi built the church between 1591 and 1602. Andrea Tirali completed the monumental classical pedimented portico in 1714. Cannonballs from the 1849 Austrian bombardment remain embedded in the facade.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Simeon Piccolo (Santi Simeone e Giuda)
Specific Location / Address: Fondamenta San Simeon Piccolo (facing Railway Station)
Description & Significance: Prominent circular domed neoclassical church greeting visitors exiting the Santa Lucia railway station, designed by Giovanni Antonio Scalfarotto.
Key Historical Context: Modeled explicitly on the Pantheon in Rome with a high green copper dome and a classical Corinthian hexastyle portico. Features an underground circular crypt with burial vaults painted with scenes of the Passion and Death.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Simeon Grande (San Simeone Profeta)
Specific Location / Address: Campo San Simeon Grande, Santa Croce
Description & Significance: Parish church overlooking a quiet campo near the Grand Canal, named 'Grande' to distinguish it from the smaller San Simeon Piccolo.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 10th century. Remodeled in 1755 by Domenico Margutti. Preserves a striking 14th-century reclining marble statue of Saint Simeon the Prophet sculpted in 1317 by a master named Marco.

Description & Significance: Grand Canal parish church featuring an exuberant late Baroque facade designed by Domenico Rossi, funded by Doge Alvise II Mocenigo.
Key Historical Context: Dedicated to Saint Eustace (Venetian 'Stae'). Doge Alvise II Mocenigo bequeathed 20,000 ducats to rebuild its facade in 1709. The interior is a museum of early 18th-century Venetian painting, featuring masterworks by Giovanni Battista Piazzetta, Sebastiano Ricci, and a youthful Giambattista Tiepolo ('Martyrdom of St. Bartholomew').

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Mater Domini
Specific Location / Address: Campo Santa Maria Mater Domini, Santa Croce
Description & Significance: Harmonious High Renaissance church designed by Mauro Codussi and Jacopo Sansovino, set on a preserved medieval campo.
Key Historical Context: Rebuilt in the early 16th century with refined Renaissance stone capitals and classical vaults. Houses celebrated paintings including Tintoretto's 'Finding of the True Cross' and Vincenzo Catena's 'Martyrdom of Saint Christina'.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Zan Degolà (San Giovanni Decollato)
Specific Location / Address: Campo San Zan Degolà, Santa Croce
Description & Significance: Rare surviving Byzantine-Romanesque parish church retaining Greek marble columns and 11th-century medieval frescoes.
Key Historical Context: Dedicated to the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist ('Zan Degolà'). Remarkably escaped complete Baroque reconstruction, preserving early medieval Romanesque brickwork, carved Byzantine capitals, and rare 11th-century frescoes of St. Helena and the Archangel Michael.

Specific Location / Address: Campo San Giacomo dall'Orio, Santa Croce
Description & Significance: One of the most atmospheric and beloved churches in Venice, featuring a 14th-century wooden ship's keel roof and a massive green Verde Antico marble column.
Key Historical Context: Name derives from 'del Lupo' (Wolf) or 'dal Lauro' (Laurel). Rebuilt in the 13th century combining Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance layers. Houses major paintings by Lorenzo Lotto, Paolo Veronese, and Francesco Bassano.

Description & Significance: Late Gothic convent church located near Piazzale Roma, named after the sharp bend (*zirada*) of the neighboring canal.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1329 by noblewomen Francesca Corraro and Elisabetta Gradenigo. Features a pristine 14th-century Gothic brick portal and works by Paolo Veneziano and Domenico Tintoretto. Survived modern highway and bus terminal constructions.

Location Name: Chiesa del Nome di Gesù (Santa Chiara)
Description & Significance: Neoclassical monastic church designed by Giannantonio Selva and completed by Antonio Diedo.
Key Historical Context: Erected in the early 19th century following the demolition of the ancient Franciscan monastery of Santa Chiara. Designed on an elegant single-nave neoclassical plan.

Specific Location / Address: Fondamenta Santa Maria Maggiore, Santa Croce
Description & Significance: Renaissance Franciscan convent church, heavily damaged and secularized in the 19th century into a military storehouse and later Venetian prison annex.
Key Historical Context: Built at the end of the 15th century with funding from patrician Alvise Malipiero. Stripped of masterworks by Veronese, Titian, and Bellini during Napoleonic looting (1806); the building was integrated into modern detention facilities.

Description & Significance: Ancient titular church that gave the entire sestiere of Santa Croce its name.
Key Historical Context: Tradition attributed its founding to the Mastropiero and Badoer families in 774. Stood along the Grand Canal until suppressed under the French in 1806 and demolished in 1810 to lay out the gardens of Villa Papadopoli.

Specific Location / Address: Isola di Santa Chiara (near Piazzale Roma)
Description & Significance: Historic Franciscan Clarisse convent church that occupied an island at the western edge of Venice.
Key Historical Context: Suppressed under French decree in 1806 and demolished in 1819 to build military barracks and modern port docks.

Location Name: Basilica di Santa Maria della Salute
Description & Significance: Grand Baroque octagonal votive basilica designed by Baldassarre Longhena, built on a platform of over one million wooden piles at the entrance of the Grand Canal.
Key Historical Context: Vowed by the Venetian Senate and Doge Nicolò Contarini on October 22, 1630, to thank the Virgin Mary for delivering Venice from the catastrophic 1630 plague that wiped out a third of the population. Celebrated annually on November 21 with a pontoon bridge across the Grand Canal (Festa della Salute). Houses Titian's ceiling canvases and Tintoretto's 'Marriage at Cana'.

Location Name: Chiesa dei Gesuati (Santa Maria del Rosario)
Description & Significance: Majestic Dominican Rococo church dominating the Zattere waterfront promenade, designed by Giorgio Massari.
Key Historical Context: Built by the Dominicans to replace the smaller neighboring church of the Gesuati. Designed by Giorgio Massari. The vault features Giambattista Tiepolo's glorious fresco cycle depicting the 'Institution of the Rosary' (1739); also houses masterworks by Sebastiano Ricci and Giambattista Piazzetta.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Carmelo (I Carmini)
Description & Significance: Large Gothic monastic church of the Carmelite friars, featuring an expansive nave lined with gilded wooden statues and a Renaissance facade by Sebastiano da Lugano.
Key Historical Context: Founded by Carmelite friars in the 13th century. Expanded in the early 16th century. In 1756, its soaring bell tower was famously straightened by engineer Giuseppe Sardi. Stands alongside the Scuola Grande dei Carmini decorated by Tiepolo.

Description & Significance: Renaissance church celebrated worldwide as the personal masterpiece temple and burial site of painter Paolo Veronese.
Key Historical Context: Designed by Antonio Abbondi (Scarpagnino). Paolo Veronese decorated the ceiling, walls, organ shutters, and presbytery across three decades (1555–1570s) with magnificent masterpieces including the 'Triumph of Mordecai' and 'Martyrdom of Saint Sebastian'. Veronese was buried inside the church beside the organ in 1588.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Trovaso (Santi Gervasio e Protasio)
Description & Significance: Parish church famous for having two identical facades (one facing the Campo and one facing the Rio) to resolve factional rivalries between the Castellani and Nicolotti.
Key Historical Context: Rebuilt in 1584 following a vault collapse. The two separate entrances allowed the bitter rival factions of the Castellani and Nicolotti to attend church without crossing paths. Houses Jacopo Tintoretto's 'Last Supper' and 'Temptation of St. Anthony'. Sits directly opposite the historic Squero di San Trovaso gondola boatyard.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Pantalon (San Pantaleone Martire)
Description & Significance: Parish church famed for the world's largest painting on canvas: a colossal illusionistic ceiling covering 443 square meters by Gian Antonio Fumiani.
Key Historical Context: Rebuilt in the late 17th century by Francesco Comin. The ceiling consists of 40 joined canvases depicting the 'Martyrdom and Glory of Saint Pantaleon', painted over 24 years (1680–1704) by Fumiani, who reputedly died falling from the scaffolding.

Description & Significance: Baroque parish church fronting the picturesque Campo San Barnaba, famous internationally as the exterior of the library in 'Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade'.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the early 9th century. Rebuilt in 1749 by Lorenzo Boschetti with a classical pedimented facade. Today serves as an exhibition space for Leonardo da Vinci engineering machine models.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Nicolò dei Mendicoli
Specific Location / Address: Campo San Nicolò dei Mendicoli, Dorsoduro
Description & Significance: One of Venice's oldest, most evocative Romanesque churches, headquarters and sacred sanctuary of the Nicolotti fishermen faction.
Key Historical Context: Surrounded by canals in the poorest fisherman quarter. Features a 15th-century exterior wooden portico (*nartece*), 12th-century Veneto-Byzantine capitals, and a sumptuous 16th-century wooden gilded iconostasis and ceiling. Historically, the fishermen gathered here to elect their leader, the Gastaldo dei Nicolotti.

Location Name: Chiesa di Sant'Angelo Raffaele (San Raffaele Arcangelo)
Description & Significance: Parish church in western Dorsoduro, renowned for its Rococo organ loft canvases depicting the Story of Tobias painted by Gianantonio Guardi.
Key Historical Context: Venetian myth claims it was founded in 416 during early barbarian invasions. Rebuilt in the 17th century by architect Francesco Contin. The organ parapet features the luminous painting series of the 'Story of Tobias' painted in the 1750s by Gianantonio Guardi (with contributions from his brother Francesco).

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Visitazione (San Gerolamo dei Gesuati)
Description & Significance: Early Renaissance church of the Gesuati friars, standing directly beside Massari's 18th-century church on the Zattere.
Key Historical Context: Built by the Poor Gesuati friars between 1494 and 1524 with a facade attributed to Mauro Codussi. Features a Renaissance coffered wooden ceiling inset with 58 painted panels of Old Testament figures and saints.

Description & Significance: Renaissance church and former convent of Augustinian nuns fronting the Giudecca Canal on the Zattere.
Key Historical Context: Built in the early 16th century. Preserves an elegant Renaissance facade and paintings by Palma il Giovane. Nearby was the historic squero and timber docks of the Zattere.

Location Name: Chiesa delle Eremite (Gesù, Maria e Giuseppe)
Description & Significance: Secluded Baroque convent church founded by the Augustinian Hermit nuns in southern Dorsoduro.
Key Historical Context: Designed by architect Giovanni Battista Lambranzi. Preserves a high Baroque altar and paintings by Pietro Ricchi.

Description & Significance: Carmelite convent church designed by Andrea Cominelli on a rigorous square plan in western Dorsoduro.
Key Historical Context: Founded for the Discalced Carmelite nuns (*Terese*). Secularized under Napoleon in 1810 and today houses an annex of the Venice School of Architecture (IUAV).

Description & Significance: Historic Gothic monastic church and Benedictine abbey positioned between the Grand Canal and the Basilica della Salute.
Key Historical Context: Reconstructed in 1461 with an elegant brick Gothic facade and stone portal. Suppressed in 1806 under the French; served for decades as the state art restoration laboratory (*Laboratorio di Restauro*).

Description & Significance: Ancient parish church located behind the Zattere, now serving as the chapel for the Cavanis Institute.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 11th century. Remodeled in the 18th century. In 1839, it was granted to the Cavanis Brothers, founders of the Congregation of the Schools of Charity.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Carità (Gallerie dell'Accademia)
Description & Significance: Former grand Gothic monastic church of the Lateran Canons, now forming the main exhibition halls of the Gallerie dell'Accademia.
Key Historical Context: Rebuilt in 1441 by Bartolomeo Bon. Converted into the Academy of Fine Arts under Napoleon in 1807; its cavernous Gothic nave was transformed into the world's premier museum of Venetian master paintings.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Basilio (San Basegio - demolished 1824)
Description & Significance: Ancient parish church that gave its name to Campo San Basegio on the Zattere, demolished in the 19th century.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 9th century by the Basegio family. Damaged by earthquake in 1347; suppressed in 1808 and demolished in 1824.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Vio (Santi Vito e Modesto - demolished 1813)
Description & Significance: Parish church celebrated in Venetian history as the site of annual dogal Thanksgiving processions commemorating the defeat of the 1310 Bajamonte Tiepolo conspiracy.
Key Historical Context: Because the dangerous aristocratic conspiracy of Bajamonte Tiepolo was crushed on Saint Vitus' Day (June 15, 1310), the Doge visited San Vio every year in solemn state procession. Demolished in 1813; a small private chapel was erected on the site in 1864.

Description & Significance: Historic parish church terminating the northern end of Campo Santa Margherita, now the central Auditorium of Ca' Foscari University.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 9th century. Closed to worship in 1810; served as a tobacco warehouse, cinema (Cinema Santa Margherita), and marble workshop before Ca' Foscari University converted it into an academic auditorium.

Location Name: Chiesa dei Catecumeni (Santa Maria dei Catecumeni)
Description & Significance: Hospice church built by the Republic to house and instruct Muslim and Jewish converts to Christianity.
Key Historical Context: Designed by Giorgio Massari in 1727. Connected directly to the public Casa dei Catecumeni established under Doge Lorenzo Priuli.

Description & Significance: Hospital church designed by Jacopo Sansovino with a famed oval hall renowned for musical acoustics and choir performances.
Key Historical Context: Founded by Saint Gaetano da Thiene to treat patients suffering from the 'incurable' French disease (syphilis). Renowned for its girl orphan choir, for whom Johann Adolf Hasse composed sacred music. Demolished in 1831.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Marta (demolished late 19th C.)
Specific Location / Address: Punta di Santa Marta (Western port area)
Description & Significance: Monastic convent church standing at the extreme western tip of Dorsoduro, demolished to construct the commercial maritime port.
Key Historical Context: Historically celebrated for the festival of Santa Marta, when Venetians traveled by boat on July 29 to eat sole and flounder (*sfogi*). Suppressed in 1806 and razed during the creation of the Stazione Marittima.

Description & Significance: Monumental votive Renaissance basilica designed by Andrea Palladio, commemorating Venice's deliverance from the devastating plague of 1575–1577.
Key Historical Context: Commissioned by the Senate and Doge Alvise I Mocenigo. Consigned to the Capuchin friars. Celebrated annually on the third Sunday of July with a historic pontoon bridge linking the Zattere to Giudecca and a magnificent fireworks display (Festa del Redentore). Preserves paintings by Tintoretto, Veronese, and Palma il Giovane.

Location Name: Chiesa delle Zitelle (Santa Maria della Presentazione)
Description & Significance: High Renaissance church and charitable hospice for impoverished young girls (*zitelle*), designed based on concepts by Andrea Palladio.
Key Historical Context: Founded by noblewomen and Jesuit father Benedetto Palmio to protect young girls from poverty and prostitution by teaching them lacemaking. Built with an imposing central dome flanked by twin bell towers.

Description & Significance: Ancient parish church of western Giudecca, retaining its Veneto-Byzantine nave, 11th-century marble columns, and a Doric portico on the canal.
Key Historical Context: One of the oldest surviving churches in the lagoon, founded in the 9th century. Contains an exterior Doric loggia built in 1596 and ceiling frescoes by Giovanni Battista Canal. Houses Bartolomeo Vivarini's signed masterpiece 'Saint Euphemia' (1480).

Description & Significance: Convent church established as a refuge and rehabilitation asylum for reformed prostitutes (*convertite*), now integrated into the Giudecca Women's Prison.
Key Historical Context: Erected through donations by Fra Bartolomeo Stella and noble patrons. Converted in the 19th century into the female penitentiary (*Carcere Femminile della Giudecca*), which remains active today.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Biagio e Cataldo (demolished 1884)
Specific Location / Address: Fondamenta San Biagio (Site of Molino Stucky)
Description & Significance: Venerable monastic church of western Giudecca demolished in 1884 to build the colossal Molino Stucky flour mill.
Key Historical Context: Given to Benedictine nuns in 1222; rebuilt in 1598 by Michele Sanmicheli's circle. Suppressed under French rule in 1810 and demolished in 1884 when Swiss entrepreneur Giovanni Stucky purchased the site to erect his industrial steam mill.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giacomo della Giudecca (demolished 1837)
Description & Significance: Servite monastery and church on central Giudecca, demolished in the 19th century to make way for industrial factories.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1338. Suppressed under the French in 1806 and demolished in 1837. In 1852, Austrian banker Salomon Mayer von Rothschild built Venice's first steam-powered asphalt and bitumen factory on its site.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Giovanni Battista della Giudecca (demolished 1844)
Description & Significance: Convent church demolished in the 19th century; replaced by residential housing and workshops.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1333. Suppressed under the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy in 1806 and demolished in 1844.

Location Name: Chiesa dei Santi Cosma e Damiano (San Cosmo - secularized)
Description & Significance: Renaissance monastic church of the Benedictine nuns, today converted into an artisan workshop and enterprise incubator.
Key Historical Context: Founded by noblewoman Marina Celsi in the late 15th century. Reconstructed in High Renaissance style with a portal designed by Mauro Codussi. Suppressed in 1810 and later used as a knitwear factory before municipal restoration.

Location Name: Chiesa della Croce (Santa Croce della Giudecca - demolished)
Description & Significance: Benedictine monastery that gave its name to the eastern promontory of Giudecca.
Key Historical Context: Suppressed in the early 19th century and converted into barracks and industrial storage before redevelopment.

Description & Significance: Triumphant Renaissance basilica and Benedictine monastery directly facing St. Mark's Basin, a supreme architectural masterpiece by Andrea Palladio.
Key Historical Context: Founded in 982 when Doge Tribuno Memmo granted the island to the Benedictines. Andrea Palladio designed the basilica in 1566, featuring an interlocking temple facade and a soaring campanile (1791) offering the iconic panorama of Venice. Houses Tintoretto's 'Last Supper' and 'The Gathering of Manna'. Venue of the 1799–1800 papal conclave that elected Pope Pius VII.

Description & Significance: Ancient cathedral of the Venetian lagoon, founded in 639, famous for its magnificent 11th-century Byzantine mosaics of the Last Judgment.
Key Historical Context: The oldest surviving monument in the lagoon, carrying an authentic foundation stone from 639. Rebuilt in 1008 under Bishop Orso Orseolo. The western wall is covered in the colossal Byzantine mosaic of the 'Last Judgment', while the central apse preserves the haunting 'Virgin Hodegetria' against a vast golden background.

Description & Significance: Centrally planned Byzantine martyrium church surrounded on five sides by an open pentagonal portico with raised stilted arches.
Key Historical Context: Built to enshrine the relics of the Virgin Martyr Santa Fosca and Saint Maura brought from Sabratha in North Africa. A premier example of Middle Byzantine lagoon architecture on a Greek-cross plan with squinches.

Location Name: Basilica dei Santi Maria e Donato (Murano)
Description & Significance: Masterpiece of Romanesque-Byzantine architecture on the glassmaking island of Murano, renowned for its two-tiered polygonal apse and 1141 mosaic floor.
Key Historical Context: Originally dedicated to Saint Mary; rededicated in 1125 when Doge Domenico Michiel brought the relics of Saint Donatus of Euroea from Cephalonia, along with the legendary bones of a dragon slain by the saint. Preserves a mosaic floor dated to 1141 depicting peacocks and eagles.

Description & Significance: Grand brick Renaissance church on Murano's main glassworking canal, acting as an art repository for treasures rescued from suppressed Murano monasteries.
Key Historical Context: Rebuilt in 1511 following a destructive fire. Holds Giovanni Bellini's famous 'Barbarigo Altarpiece' (1488) and 'Assumption', Paolo Veronese's 'St. Jerome in the Desert', and monumental chandeliers blown by master Murano glassmakers.

Location Name: Chiesa di Santa Maria degli Angeli (Murano)
Description & Significance: Monastic convent church of wealthy patrician nuns, renowned for its carved gilded ceiling and Jacopo Tintoretto's 'Finding of the Body of Saint Mark'.
Key Historical Context: Favored by Venetian doges and foreign royalty; King Henry III of France visited in 1574. Preserves Tintoretto's altarpiece and paintings by Palma il Giovane.

Description & Significance: Parish church of the lacemaking island of Burano, dominating the lagoon skyline with its dramatically leaning 53-meter campanile.
Key Historical Context: Built on a Latin-cross plan with an unfinished facade. Renowned for its severely tilting 17th-century bell tower and Giambattista Tiepolo's masterpiece 'Crucifixion' (1725).

Description & Significance: Atmospheric Gothic monastic church on the orchard island of Mazzorbo, housing the oldest church bell in the Venetian lagoon (cast in 1318).
Key Historical Context: Built for Benedictine nuns. Features a Gothic ship's keel roof and a 14th-century relief above the portal. The campanile bell cast in 1318 is recognized as the oldest working bell in the entire Venetian estuary.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Nicolò del Lido
Specific Location / Address: Riviera San Nicolò, Lido di Venezia
Description & Significance: Historic abbey church guarding the maritime Porto di Lido entrance, destination of the annual Ascension Day dogal Marriage of the Sea (*Sposalizio del Mare*).
Key Historical Context: Founded in 1044. Venetian crusaders brought relics of Saint Nicholas of Myra here in 1099. Every Ascension Day, the Doge sailed out aboard the golden Bucintoro to the Porto di Lido off San Nicolò to throw a consecrated gold ring into the sea, declaring 'Desponsamus te, mare' (We wed thee, sea).

Description & Significance: Historical parish church greeting passengers arriving at the primary waterbus terminal of the Lido.
Key Historical Context: Built in the early 17th century to serve the agricultural and fisherman hamlet of the Lido before its late 19th-century transformation into an international beach resort.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Michele in Isola
Specific Location / Address: Isola di San Michele (Venice Cemetery Island)
Description & Significance: The first Renaissance church erected in Venice, a masterpiece of white Istrian stone architecture designed by Mauro Codussi on the cemetery island.
Key Historical Context: Commissioned by the Camaldolese monks. Mauro Codussi designed the groundbreaking rusticated Renaissance facade and interior based on Leon Battista Alberti's classical principles. The island was designated as Venice's central monumental cemetery in 1837 under French and Austrian decrees.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Lazzaro degli Armeni
Specific Location / Address: Isola di San Lazzaro degli Armeni
Description & Significance: Monastic headquarters and international printing center of the Armenian Catholic Mechitarist Order, visited by Lord Byron in 1816.
Key Historical Context: Granted to Abbot Mechitar and Armenian monks fleeing Ottoman persecution in Morea in 1717. Preserves an extensive museum of oriental manuscripts, Egyptian mummies, an Armenian printing press, and Lord Byron's study room.

Description & Significance: Island monastery church designed by Tommaso Temanza for the Hospitaller Order of the Fatebenefratelli on Venice's historic psychiatric hospital island.
Key Historical Context: Founded in the 9th century. In 1725, it was assigned to the Fatebenefratelli to operate a military hospital, which became Venice's central psychiatric institution in the 18th and 19th centuries. Now houses Venice International University.

Description & Significance: Historic monastic church situated on the private island of San Clemente, now an exclusive luxury resort.
Key Historical Context: Founded as a hospice for crusaders and pilgrims by Pietro Gattilesso in 1131. In 1643, Venetian patricians funded the erection of a replica of the Holy House of Loreto inside the church nave.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Francesco del Deserto
Specific Location / Address: Isola di San Francesco del Deserto
Description & Significance: Secluded Franciscan lagoon monastery surrounded by cypress trees, founded where Saint Francis of Assisi took refuge during a lagoon storm in 1220.
Key Historical Context: Tradition holds that Saint Francis of Assisi landed here on his return from the Fifth Crusade in 1220 and prayed with the singing birds. Granted to the Franciscans by Jacopo Michiel in 1233; remains an active friary.

Description & Significance: Magnificent Carthusian monastery church whose Renaissance portal was carved by Pietro Lombardo.
Key Historical Context: Expanded in 1449 with lavish chapels of noble Venetian families. Pietro Lombardo designed the famous Cappella dei Gussoni. Suppressed under French decree in 1810 and demolished in 1812 to establish military munitions works and artillery barracks.

Specific Location / Address: Isola di San Secondo (Lagoon between Venice and Mestre)
Description & Significance: Ancient island convent church of Benedictine and Dominican nuns, demolished to construct an Austrian military fort.
Key Historical Context: Relics of Saint Secundus were enshrined here in 1113. Suppressed in 1806 and demolished during the 19th century to build the Napoleonic-Austrian lagoon defensive fort guarding the railway bridge.

Location Name: Chiesa di San Vitale di Poveglia (demolished 1800s)
Description & Significance: Historic parish church of the prosperous ancient island community of Poveglia; its standalone bell tower survives today as a landmark lighthouse.
Key Historical Context: Poveglia was an independent civic community governed by its own castaldo until devastated during the War of Chioggia (1379). Suppressed under French rule; the church was demolished, leaving only the 12th-century campanile, later used as a navigational beacon and quarantine station.

Location Name: Chiesa della Madonna di Punta Marina (Lido / San Servolo)
Description & Significance: Modern votive maritime church dedicated to the Virgin of Punta Marina, consecrated during World War II.
Key Historical Context: Inaugurated on September 14, 1941, during World War II as a coastal sanctuary for sailors, coastal artillery guards, and residents of the Lido and lagoon shores.
